lesson.title: Merci & Bonjour Gym
lesson.subtitle: Greetings, thanks, s'il vous plaît — the politeness set in dialogue drills.

hook.title: Politeness as a Complete French Circuit
hook.content: Every interaction in a shop, bakery, or café opens with Bonjour ! Add s'il vous plaît ('if it pleases you') and merci beaucoup ('thank you very much') to complete the politeness circuit.

footnotes.title: Why s'il vous plaît adapts to s'il te plaît with a friend
footnotes.content: When speaking to one friend (tu), the indirect pronoun inside s'il vous plaît simply switches from vous to te: s'il te plaît!

pattern.title: Bonjour → Request + S'il vous plaît → Merci
pattern.content: Chain the three politeness beats in order.
pattern.linguist_note: Politeness formulas in French preserve fossilized conditional syntax (s'il vous plaît = 'if it pleases to-you').
pattern.trap_note: Never forget the circumflex î on plaît!

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a polite café exchange:

matching_pairs.english: Please (formal, lit. if it pleases you)

exercises.target_answer: Bonjour, s'il vous plaît, s'il te plaît, merci beaucoup
exercises.meaning: Good day / Hello (opening key), Please (formal, lit. if it pleases you), Please (informal, to a friend), Thank you very much
exercises.explanation: Every polite exchange starts with Bonjour.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word meaning of 's'il vous plaît'?
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: if it to-you pleases

exercises.target_answer: Bonjour, un café, s'il vous plaît
exercises.explanation: Open with Bonjour, name the item, close with s'il vous plaît.

exercises.idea: yes thank you it is very good
cues: it is very good → c'est très bon
exercises.meaning: Yes, thank you, it is very good
exercises.explanation: Oui, merci, c'est très bon is a natural response at the table.

diagnosis.cue: Use c'est très bon for 'it is very good'.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Bonjour, vous avez une table, s'il vous plaît
exercises.target_answer: Bonjour, vous avez une table, s'il vous plaît
exercises.meaning: Hello, do you have a table, please?
exercises.explanation: Rising voice turns vous avez une table into a polite question.
exercises.affirmation: You chained Bonjour, vous avez une table, and s'il vous plaît.

summary.outcome: Conduct complete polite exchanges using Bonjour, s'il vous/te plaît, and merci.

use_example.german: Bonjour ! Un thé, s'il vous plaît. — Merci !
use_example.english: Hello! A tea, please. — Thank you!

summary.takeaway: Always open with Bonjour before asking a question in France.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([902] The vous Register): see how Merci & Bonjour Gym leads directly into The vous Register.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "Hello, a coffee, please" in French:
twist.target_answer: Bonjour, un café, s'il vous plaît
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Bonjour, un café, s'il vous plaît" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Merci & Bonjour Gym.

bonjour.etymology_derivation: bon 'good' + jour 'day' (Latin diurnum) — English's 'good day' is the same thought, German's Guten Tag too.

merci.etymology_derivation: Latin mercēs 'wages, reward' — thank-you and mercy are the same coin: what you owe.

oui.etymology_derivation: worn down from Vulgar Latin hoc illud 'yes indeed!' — a yes so emphatic it wore itself into one syllable.

sil_vous_plait.etymology_derivation: 'if it pleases you' — politeness as a small conditional; compare 'if you please', which English still owns.

vous.etymology_derivation: Latin vōs 'you all' promoted to politeness — the same T–V ladder as German Sie and English's lost 'ye'.

tu.etymology_derivation: Latin tū — the very word the King James Bible still whispers as thou. Point your lips; the vowel is not English's.

voudrais.context_phrase: Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
voudrais.context_translation: I would like a croissant, please.
voudrais.etymology_derivation: Future stem voudr- + imparfait ending -ais = the polite conditional!

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → French café. English took the same journey twice: coffee and café.
